definition: Reading attention weights as evidence about what a model is using, across 7 sources both a productive signal and a repeatedly qualified one. Its productive uses here are comparative rather than absolute: attention paid to the end-of-thinking token from that position ranks which reasoning steps matter, validated by ablation showing that pruning the highest-ranked steps spikes the answer's perplexity while pruning the lowest raises it marginally and random pruning falls between; and cross-phase routing focus separates reasoning hallucinations. Its recurring qualification is that attention says where a model looked, not what it found -- one hallucination study finds attention alone does not separate real from hallucinated objects and only what the attended region decodes to does, and another notes that a circuit analysis operating mostly at the level of attention patterns would be better strengthened by embedding-level analysis. The archive's standing note applies: high attention correlated with a downstream quantity is a correlation between one position and one measurement, not evidence that information is routed through that position causally.

evidence.note: Refutes the standard account of vision-language hallucination -- that the model attends too little to the image -- by showing real and hallucinated objects draw equally strong attention, then uses a logit lens over the attended regions to separate two causally distinct hallucination types and treat each differently.
evidence.title: Same Attention, Different Truths: Put Logit-Lens over Visual Attention to Detect and Mitigate LVLM Object Hallucination

evidence.note: Reads a frozen vision-language model's forward pass as a structured computational trace -- a graph over image patches, query tokens and generated tokens with attention as edges, processed by interleaved relational, spatial and sequential modules -- and shows that structuring the same internals prior detectors already read lifts hallucination detection from a 69-75 AUC plateau to 90.
evidence.title: UniProbe: A Learnable Token-Level Hallucination Detector for Large VLMs using Multi-Structural Internal Representations

evidence.note: An inference-time safeguard that reads a reasoning model's attention to find key points in its reasoning path and injects safety reflections there, then scales sampling to pick a safe path.
evidence.title: ReasoningGuard: Safeguarding Large Reasoning Models with Inference-time Safety Aha Moments

evidence.note: A benchmark where each task needs one commonsense step and one math step, on which model accuracy drops nearly 30% relative to solving the steps in isolation while humans show no such gap.
evidence.title: AgentCoMa: A Compositional Benchmark Mixing Commonsense and Mathematical Reasoning in Real-World Scenarios

evidence.note: Detects reasoning hallucinations by measuring how strongly cross-step attention routing aligns with hidden-state semantic proximity, finding that higher alignment means higher hallucination risk.
evidence.title: RFS-Guard: Detecting Reasoning Hallucinations via Cross-Phase Routing Focus in Large Reasoning Models

evidence.note: Finds that the </think> token aggregates the reasoning chain in deep layers and that attention paid to it from that position ranks which steps matter, then uses that ranking to drive a four-operator compression search — cutting 58% of tokens with accuracy holding.
evidence.title: CRISP: Compressing Redundancy in Chain-of-Thought via Intrinsic Saliency Pruning

evidence.note: Gives the first optimization guarantee that gradient descent trains constant-depth transformers to solve NC1-complete problems with chain of thought, and shows the algebraic structure of the task decides how far the learned reasoning extrapolates.
evidence.title: Transformers Provably Learn Chain-of-Thought Reasoning with Length Generalization

name: attention analysis
